title: Assyrtiko
description: Santorini's grape: bone-dry, steely and saline, keeping high acidity in fierce sun.
L: Assyrtiko gives bone-dry whites with lemon, lime, grapefruit, flint and a saline, smoky mineral edge. Acidity is very high, often with pH around 3, and alcohol can be high, 13.5 to 14.5%. Body is medium to full. It's Greece's most famous white grape.

Most grapes lose acidity in hot climates. Assyrtiko is unusual: it keeps very high acidity even when fully ripe under intense Aegean sun. Its tartaric acid is especially stable. This makes it valuable as the climate warms, and it's been planted in Australia, South Africa and the US.
It keeps high acidity even in hot climates
It only grows in cold places
Few grapes keep such acidity under strong sun.

Look for pale lemon colour, citrus, flint and a sea-salt character, a firm, steely palate with high acidity and fairly high alcohol, and a long, mineral finish. Compared with Riesling, it's less floral and more saline and smoky.
Assyrtiko loses most of its acidity in hot climates.
Not true. It keeps high acidity even in intense heat.

Assyrtiko's home is Santorini, a volcanic island in the Aegean, formed by a huge eruption around 1600 BC. Its soil, called aspa, is volcanic ash, pumice and lava, with almost no clay or organic matter. Rainfall is very low, about 300 mm a year; vines rely on night sea mist for moisture. Strong winds blow constantly.

Santorini's volcanic sand doesn't let phylloxera survive, so the vines are ungrafted. Some root systems are over 400 years old: growers cut old vines back and let new shoots grow from the same roots. Assyrtiko also grows in mainland Greece, Macedonia and Crete, and in Australia's Clare Valley.

On Santorini, Assyrtiko is often blended with Athiri and Aidani, two aromatic local grapes. Santorini PDO must be at least 75% Assyrtiko. Single-vineyard and old-vine bottlings, like Nykteri, made from grapes picked at night, are increasingly common.
Phylloxera can't survive in its volcanic soil
Phylloxera can't survive in Santorini's volcanic sand.
Santorini's volcanic aspa soil and sea mist shape Assyrtiko
Ungrafted roots can be over 400 years old
It also grows in mainland Greece, Crete and Australia

On Santorini, vines are trained into low baskets, called kouloura, woven from their own canes, lying on the ground. The grapes grow inside the basket. Each year the basket grows; after decades, growers cut it back and start again from the old roots. It's one of the oldest training systems in the world.

The kouloura protects grapes from Santorini's strong winds, which can reach over 50 km/h, and from fierce sun and sand. Inside, the grapes catch night humidity from sea mist, the vines' main water source. The low shape keeps the vines close to the ground, where it's cooler and more humid.
What does the kouloura protect against?
Santorini has mild winters; frost isn't the main concern.

Santorini's yields are among the lowest in Europe, often 10 to 20 hectolitres per hectare, compared with 50 or more elsewhere. Old roots, drought and wind keep them low. Combined with steep land prices from tourism, this makes Santorini expensive and its vineyards endangered.

Santorini's Vinsanto is a sweet wine made from at least 51% Assyrtiko, with Aidani. Grapes are picked late and dried in the sun for 12 to 14 days, concentrating sugar. The must ferments slowly, and the wine ages for at least two years in oak, often much longer.

Vinsanto can age 10, 20 or even 50 years in barrel, becoming deep amber to dark brown, with raisin, dried apricot, coffee, caramel and spice. Assyrtiko's acidity keeps it fresh despite very high sugar, often over 200 g/l. Its name may come from Santo, for Santorini, wine of Santorini.
How are grapes for Santorini Vinsanto concentrated?
Dried in the sun for 12 to 14 days

Santorini's Vinsanto and Tuscany's Vin Santo share a name but differ. Tuscan Vin Santo uses Trebbiano and Malvasia dried indoors and ages in sealed caratelli. Santorini's uses Assyrtiko dried in the sun. The name's origin may link to Santorini or to holy wine, vino santo.
Santorini Vinsanto and Tuscan Vin Santo use the same grapes.
Not true. Santorini uses Assyrtiko and Aidani; Tuscany uses Trebbiano and Malvasia.
It ages for years, becoming amber with raisin and coffee
It differs from Tuscan Vin Santo in grapes and method

Dry Assyrtiko suits Greek food: grilled octopus, sea bass, shellfish, fava, Santorini's yellow split pea purée, tomato fritters and feta. Its acidity cuts through olive oil and fried food. Its saline edge suits oysters and sushi too.

Serve dry Assyrtiko at 8 to 11 degrees. It ages surprisingly well thanks to its acidity: top Santorini wines develop over 10 to 15 years, gaining smoky, honeyed notes. Vinsanto, served at 12 to 14, suits dried fruit, nuts, blue cheese and chocolate.
Its acidity and salinity suit grilled seafood.
